source.title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
source.authors: Zi-Xi Chen; Akshay Vegesna; Samip Dahal; Andrew Gordon Wilson

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits compute-optimal validation-loss scaling laws and tests extrapolation, using loss-versus-compute measurements comparable to the original scaling-law method, but on architectural variants and training recipes.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own validation-loss scaling fits, loss-matched compute comparisons, held-out extrapolation, compute-optimal token allocation, shape comparisons, and downstream forecasts. The paper also reports many tuning grids and ablations; values used only to choose hyperparameters or architecture settings are not recorded as results rows unless the paper explicitly reports their effect on scaling, loss, or allocation.
record.test_reason: The study fits Chinchilla-style compute-optimal loss-versus-compute power laws (Eq. 1, Huber-fitted floor) and iso-compute tokens-per-parameter optima, then tests extrapolation on a held-out larger run. That is the original method and measure, applied across eight architecture ladders spanning 10^18–10^20 FLOPs. Its central result is that architecture and recipe change the fitted exponent.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that model growth and a boundary operator raise the compute-optimal pretraining exponent, while untying weights improves only the constant. The fitted laws predict a held-out run at 8× the fitted compute, in both loss and CORE. Architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning is needed, or exponent gains can be hidden. In multi-epoch data-constrained training, the optimal loop count rises with compute, and loop scaling beats parameter scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Uses compute-optimal loss-versus-compute power-law fitting and held-out extrapolation, but compares purpose-designed transformer architectures and architecture-specific recipes rather than reproducing the original model-size/token scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling advantage changes with architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning, corpus, shape and scaling direction. Transferring Vanilla's recipe to Operator-1 hides its exponent improvement; width-only scaling yields a constant rather than exponent advantage for the fixed-depth comparison. The paper also reports that boundary-operator allocation and model-growth timing affect outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Architectural interventions (a boundary operator that normalises and re-injects the prelude output, and mid-training depth growth) raise the compute-optimal loss exponent from 0.111 to 0.114–0.117. Untying weights changes only the constant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal scaling exponents of transformer pretraining loss can be increased by architectural changes, not just the constant.

fits_no_version.finding: With 100M unique tokens repeated for ten epochs, the loss-minimising loop count rises with compute. Loop scaling matches the best weight-decay-tuned model-size scaling with 2.2× less compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under data repetition, increasing tied loop count is a more compute-efficient way to add capacity than increasing stored model size.

record.problems: The main scaling ladders cover about 10^18–10^20 FLOPs; extrapolation beyond that range is demonstrated with one held-out large Untied-Grow run. The GPT-3 comparison uses different training data and a separate evaluation pipeline, and is described by the authors as indicative rather than controlled. Downstream accuracy is less smooth than answer NLL. The loss-law fits share an irreducible loss fitted on Vanilla.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out under the 60-row cap. Numerous tuning-grid values and architectural-choice sweeps used only to select settings are omitted under the gate rules.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in parameters or in tokens with the other factor non-limiting; only compute-optimal ladders over about two orders of magnitude are fitted.
Extrapolation over several orders of magnitude. The held-out run is about 8× (under one order) beyond the fit, for one architecture (Untied-Grow) only.
Separate power-law exponents for N and T, and the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann contrast. The TPP stability test spans five budgets d8–d12, roughly a 5× compute range.
Systematic shape sweeps at fixed parameter count, and details other than depth/width.
Entire version: no other modality, fine-tuning or transfer regime. The second corpus is still text pretraining.
Downstream tasks beyond DCLM CORE; held-out downstream forecast for only one run.

missing.what: Learning-rate scaling rule changes the Vanilla ladder exponent: constant recipe 0.0974 vs GLR-scaled 0.1106 (muP OM-only 0.0977).
Optimizer choice changes the exponent: Adam 0.1169 vs Muon 0.1112 under coupled width/depth scaling, but 0.1020 vs 0.1053 under width-only scaling.
Constant base recipes reorder architectures and change apparent exponents (e.g. Vanilla 0.1644 vs Loop Grow 0.1988 in Fig. 15c legend).
Optimal TPP for growth variants (tied 6.39→6.97, untied 7.43→8.97 in 6T^2/C), showing compute-optimal allocation depends on schedule.
Optimal TPP differs by architecture: rounded 5 for Vanilla, 6 with operator, 7–8 with growth.

record.verdict_notes: The record linked r22–r23 to V5 and gave a V5 supports label while its own version status called V5 not tested. A second text corpus is not V5, so the label is dropped and the rows relinked to V1/V7. All loss-law fits share an irreducible floor fitted on Vanilla, itself a fitting choice. The extrapolation span (8×) is short of V2's 'orders of magnitude'. The TPP stability tests cover only about a 5× compute range and rest on non-rejection. Optimal TPP (5–6) is far below Chinchilla's ~20, but the paper does not compare against it.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss against compute along compute-optimal ladders; it does not independently vary parameters or tokens while holding the other quantities fixed.
Tests one held-out Untied-Grow run beyond the fitted compute range, not large-scale extrapolation for every architecture or setup.

Tests whether compute-optimal tokens per stored parameter drift across budgets for several architectures. It does not fit separate power-law exponents for parameter count and token count, nor test the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison as such.
Tests selected depth-to-width and width-only comparisons; it does not sweep a wide range of architecture details at fixed parameter count.

No other modality, fine-tuning, or transfer regime is tested for the same power-law form. The corpus comparison remains text pretraining; repeated-data results test loop allocation and overfitting, not whether a single power-law loss form holds.
Tests downstream CORE metrics and forecasts on the reported tasks and checkpoints, not all downstream tasks or capability measures.

Tests dependence on recipe, corpus, architecture shape, and some fitting choices. It does not systematically compare all parameter-counting conventions, datasets, schedules, or fitting methods in the original studies.

rows.subject: Operator-1
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss-matched compute against Vanilla across the measured ladder.

rows.value: Increases from 1.12× at 10^18 FLOPs to 1.25× at 10^20 FLOPs
rows.note: Authors interpret the increasing multiplier as an exponent improvement.
rows.check: A compute multiplier is not a test of the power-law form. It shows the fitted exponent differing by architecture (boundary operator), so it bears on setup-dependence of exponents, not V1.

rows.note: The paper contrasts this exponent improvement with the fixed-factor advantage of untying over Loop-2.

rows.subject: Deep Vanilla
rows.operation_detail: Compared a deeper shape with Vanilla at compute-matched loss.
rows.measure: Compute multiplier over Vanilla at matched loss
rows.value: Flat near 1.08×
rows.note: The paper attributes this constant gain to a more favorable width–depth ratio.
rows.check: Not at fixed parameter count: the comparison is compute-matched, and Deep Vanilla stores more blocks at a smaller width-depth ratio. The gain is a constant 1.08×, which the authors explicitly call contrary to Kaplan. Modest but not negligible.

source_check.correct: The rule is width = 128 × nominal depth. Deep Vanilla executes P + 2C + D blocks, giving a smaller actual width-to-depth ratio than Vanilla. Its loss-matched compute multiplier is approximately 1.08×. For V4, state = cannot_determine: the comparison does not hold parameter count fixed.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3; Section 4.2, deeper-shape comparison; Table 1; Figure 3 caption.
source_check.problem: The condition confuses nominal with actual depth, and a compute-efficiency comparison cannot establish partial failure of fixed-parameter V4.

rows.subject: Untied-2
rows.operation_detail: Compared width-only scaling at fixed executed depth with coupled width-and-depth scaling.
rows.measure: Scaling advantage over Deep Vanilla

rows.subject: Operator-1 with Vanilla recipe
rows.operation_detail: Transferred Vanilla's tuned hyperparameters to Operator-1 instead of using architecture-specific tuning.
